title: Republic of Ireland: Public sector strike begins
description: Hundreds of thousands of workers on strike across Republic of IrelandImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The strike action will last 24 hoursByAdam M
body: Hundreds of thousands of workers on strike across Republic of IrelandImage source, PA MediaImage caption, The strike action will last 24 hoursByAdam MandevilleBBC News NIUpdated 8 hours agoMore than 300,000 workers, including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants, are on strike across the Republic of Ireland.It comes amid an ongoing pay dispute between public sector workers and the Irish government, with a further strike planned on 21 October. It is expected schools could be closed with hospital appointments cancelled and picket lines formed across the country during the 24-hour strike.At the end of September, more than 100,000 workers, including nurses, school staff and civil servants, moved to work-to-rule measures.At the start of October, primary and secondary school teachers in the Republic began work-to-rule action.Previously almost 97% of Fórsa members, who voted in an industrial ballot, did so in favour of action. It is the Republic's biggest public service union.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Strike action is taking place across the Republic of IrelandBrendan O'Brien divisional organiser of SIPTU, which represents public sector health and administration workers, previously said the "goodwill" of workers was a large part of what kept public services going.However, he said the Irish government's failure to establish a basis for formal talks "left our members with no alternative but to act collectively".On Tuesday Jack Chambers, the Republic's minister for expenditure, described the strike action as "deeply disappointing" saying it would cause significant disruption to the economy, with thousands of hospital appointments set to be cancelled and schools closed.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Public sector workers outside Leinster House in DublinDawn Hutchings-Walsh is a teacher at Hartstown Community School in Dublin, and commutes from County Wicklow every day.Speaking to Irish broadcaster RTÉ she said the "pay just isn't stretching the way that it used to".Her colleague Sinéad McCarthy said she had to take a career break and move to Dubai for a couple of years to save money for a deposit."It's just not feasible in Ireland to be able to save for a house considering the circumstances and the money that we are on here in this country," she said.Linda Kelly is the general secretary of the Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland (ASTI) said teachers are "really struggling in terms of their pay"."They don't feel like the government is taking them seriously, there's a lot of disappointment with the laissez-faire approach from government over the last couple of months."There's been ample time to solve this issue and the government has sat on its hands and this is the result now," Kelly told RTÉ.

schema.headline: Republic of Ireland: Public sector strike begins

title: Starlink: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds
description: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connecte
body: Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on."Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said."Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".The US government has not commented.While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military. Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit."It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities. Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed after the US made a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel."Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed.During his one-day visit, Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles.Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones."We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky.

schema.headline: Starlink: Musk says US government may be behind slowdown of Ukraine drone speeds

title: Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
description: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosisByMaia Davies and Sarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentRe
body: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosisByMaia Davies and Sarah RainsfordSouthern and Eastern Europe correspondentReporting fromRomePope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican.The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy.The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery."After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital.The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers.He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread.The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis's hospital visits.Pope Leo's predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life.Figure caption, Pope Leo announced on Sunday that he would undergo surgery to remove a growth on his lungWhat is lung adenocarcinoma?Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer.The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades.Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

schema.headline: Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say

title: Kenya confirms second Ebola case - a relative of the first victim
description: Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the D
body: Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola, 10 days after a businessman died of the virus after he had travelled to the East African nation from the Democratic Republic of Congo.The new patient, a 39-year-old man, is a close relative of the first case and was already in quarantine when he fell ill on Tuesday, Kenya's health ministry says.The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.Detecting his illness early had improved his chances of recovery and limited the chance of him passing the virus on to others, the ministry said, as it urged the public to "stay calm but vigilant"."Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," the ministry said."Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings", it added.The 40-year-old Kenyan man who died on 5 October was diagnosed with Ebola shortly after being admitted to hospital in the capital, Nairobi.A relative had taken him there shortly after picking him up at the airport. He had travelled from DR Congo, through Uganda to Kenya without his illness being detected.Since his death, officials had determined that he had been in contact with 128 people - and since Tuesday 113 of them had been found, the health ministry said.Of these, 108 were in quarantine in Kenya and tracing of the remaining 15 continued, it said.More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit."Anyone with fever, unusual tiredness, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding should seek care promptly at the nearest health facility," Kenya's health ministry said.The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent's leading public health agency, has reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements for the six weeks leading up to his death.It revealed that he first started feeling unwell in DR Congo on 15 September - and showed how several opportunities to detect the infection were missed, including during several visits to Congolese medical facilities.He then managed to travel through Uganda to Kenya - and was again not detected at airports screenings.Health experts say it highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

schema.headline: Kenya confirms second Ebola case - a relative of the first victim

title: Albania protests: Student protesters attack government ministries in Tirana
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The scene in Tirana, Albania's capital on WednesdayByRachel FlynnThousands of students have taken to the streets i
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The scene in Tirana, Albania's capital on WednesdayByRachel FlynnThousands of students have taken to the streets in the Albanian capital of Tirana, attacking several government buildings on the second day of violent anti-government protests.The demonstration began outside the ministry of education on Tuesday, as students called for better university conditions and job prospects. Wednesday saw part of the education ministry's building set on fire, while the prime minister's office, finance and interior ministry, and several surrounding businesses were also attacked.Albania's Deputy Prime Minister ​Albana Koçiu has called for "calmness, self-restraint and maturity" and said "Albania does not need to burn to change".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Dozens of protesters wearing gas masks and balaclavas were seen throwing rocks and firecrackers through the education ministry's gatesRiot police have clashed with the protesters, using tear gas and water cannons to disperse them. One demonstrator, Enida Bimi, told Reuters news agency that the protest is not just for the students, but "for all the people of Albania". "The people are very angry at the system. They need to change everything. With this corruption all around, the crime and everything else is happening. And the people now are angry. They need to change the system," Bimi said. Another protester, Arber Leshi, said people are angry at "the most corrupt government our country has ever seen".  Education Mirela Kumbaro said that while she respects the right to protest, "civic student protest and violence against public buildings and property are two different things".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protester Enida Bimi said people "are very angry at the system"Officials have criticised the behaviour of some protesters."Setting fire to an institution is not a peaceful protest. It is an act that endanger's peoples lives", said economy minister Delina Ibrahimaj, responding to a video appearing to show protesters throwing rocks at the finance ministry building.Sixteen people were arrested "in connection with violent acts" during Tuesday's protest, Albania's state-run news agency said. Sali Berisha, the leader of the opposition - the Democratic Party of Albania - has praised the protesters. "The streets and squares of Tirana have never seen lions like these students," he said during an evening meeting on Wednesday, Albania's state-run news agency Ata reported.This student-led protest comes after months of anti-government protests, known as the Flamingo Revolution, which is calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. The protests were sparked by a luxury tourism project linked to Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency from Rama's government.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Central Tirana on Wednesday evening

schema.headline: Albania protests: Student protesters attack government ministries in Tirana

title: Australia’s first Michelin stars awarded to 11 restaurants
description: Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction.Magill Estate Resta
body: Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction.Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each.South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country.Magill chef and owner Scott Huggins said he had "dreamt of working in Michelin star restaurants as a youngster".He said he had worked in Michelin star restaurants in Europe and Japan."It's one thing working for one, one thing achieving two [Michelin stars]," he said.Wednesday's announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and following years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia.Michelin has approached the national tourism board about bringing the guide to the country more than once, with no luck.South Australia decided to go it alone and pursued its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with ABC News."It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said.The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion.

schema.headline: Australia’s first Michelin stars awarded to 11 restaurants

title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
description: A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dra
body: A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history.Prosecutors say Serhii Kuznetsov played a leading role in a team of saboteurs that destroyed the pipelines, accusing him of a war crime. His defence has called for the case to be dismissed.The case is highly sensitive in Germany, one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.Extradited to Germany last year, Kuznetsov denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.Kuznetsov became the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts on Wednesday morning, and a packed public gallery looked on as he entered the courtroom, appearing relaxed.He even smiled at times, including during initial exchanges where he spoke to confirm personal details such as his name and place of birth.He had previously only been identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K and pictured with his face blurred, but a court spokeswoman said he had now waived his anonymity.Kuznetsov, 50, wore a pair of headphones and appeared to listen intently to a translation of proceedings in Ukrainian, as the prosecution read out the charges against him of ordering divers and an explosive expert to attack civilian infrastructure. The defence outlined their case, telling the court that only circumstantial evidence had emerged in the four years since the Nord Stream blasts. "[Prosecutors] made a thorough investigation of four years," Italian defence lawyer Nicola Canestrini told the BBC outside the courtroom. "They did not find one single witness, they did not find no forensics, no DNA, no fingerprints - nothing!"In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock. They said later that  "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction, external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".In August 2025, Kuznetsov was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, when his surname emerged in court documents, Kuznetsov was transferred to Germany late last year.German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

schema.headline: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines

title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
description: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly
body: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals.The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce.Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to".The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers.In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation".Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount.Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources." Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon". The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October.Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series.It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films.However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer.He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau."Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said.The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.

schema.headline: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022

title: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?
description: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air f
body: Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized."Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network.Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said.Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need.The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine.Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.President Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk.Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and  Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX.Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.And in a post on X, external, Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology."Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train, but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.

schema.headline: Ukraine war: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield?

title: Saudi employee charged with planting recording device at OpenAI office
description: A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. A
body: A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room. OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired. According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier". According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customising, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege. He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customis[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".

schema.headline: Saudi employee charged with planting recording device at OpenAI office

title: Andy Burnham says he wants to 'repair bridges' between Ukraine and US
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States, ahead of a meeting with President Volodymy
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States, ahead of a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street.The Ukrainian president was welcomed by a military ceremonial guard outside Number 10 as he arrived for the meeting, in what is thought to be a first for a foreign leader.It comes after President Donald Trump said he had struck a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel.Asked about Trump's move during Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham resisted criticising the US president, saying he wanted to "be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together".However, he stressed that Zelensky would not be leaving the UK "empty-handed", as he said further military and financial support would be drawn up in the coming weeks.Burnham is expected to use the visit to promise further sanctions against Russia, while also announcing the UK will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).It is Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister. While other world leaders have received military welcomes, Number 10 said it could not find a record of one taking place on Downing Street.During PMQs, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey asked whether he agreed the diesel deal was "yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security".In response, Burnham did not echo Sir Ed's condemnation of Trump, saying: "What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back and therefore I should at this moment in time be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."The PM said he had spoken to Zelensky over the phone on Saturday "because I recognised it was another very dark and difficult moment for him as they contemplate a winter that will be severe for his people".The phone call came after Trump announced that President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US, as he suspended sanctions on diesel from Moscow.Zelensky branded the move a gift to Putin, warning it would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against Ukraine.Trump responded by saying it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".Meanwhile, Zelensky has said at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes.He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit – despite Trump's claim on Sunday that a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure was in place between Russia and Ukraine.Russia said its strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.Zelensky has said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same.But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham says he wants to 'repair bridges' between Ukraine and US

title: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer
description: Image source, Reuters/DOJImage caption, A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)ByLaura CressTechnology reporterA
body: Image source, Reuters/DOJImage caption, A recording device (R) was wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a TV (L)ByLaura CressTechnology reporterA Saudi national who worked for OpenAI appeared in court this week for allegedly planting a secret recording device behind a TV in one of the tech giant's meeting rooms. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, was arrested by the FBI and charged with using or attempting to use a device "to intercept oral communications".As yet, it is not clear what he was planning to do with the recordings. But, here's we do know so far.Help from a chatbotThe engineer asked AI to help him listen in to discussions about AI, according to an official complaint (the document filed in court).Between 17 August and 16 September, Alfozan had reportedly asked a productivity AI assistant several questions about meeting rooms and their availability.Some detailed in the complaint include "how about external partners, where would they usually meet with OpenAI at" and "can you list today's meeting in this room".The complaint also claimed that in September, Alfozan used a chatbot associated with his spouse to ask how to build and install a recording device and how to access it remotely.Alfozan had worked at the firm for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant a recorder.The room where the device was found was regularly used to hold meetings to discuss "highly confidential technical, commercial and strategic information" as well as OpenAI's "government engagements and commercial relationships", the complaint stated.Alfozan had no authority to access or be involved with meetings in the room, the complaint states.But CCTV footage recorded him near the conference room on eight separate occasions in September.Hiding in plain toilet paperOn 30 September, OpenAI staff discovered a "surreptitious audio recording device" behind a television - which had been wrapped in toilet paper. A camera was placed in the conference room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering the room and appeared to look behind the television where the device had been inserted.The complaint also stated that same day he allegedly left an unattended bag in a different room.When security personnel opened it, it was found to contain "another recording device" similar to the one discovered, as well as Alfozan's wallet and ID.In a post on X, external, OpenAI wrote it had used its own AI models to "understand the device and where it had come from".It also said: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data."Image source, Reuters/DOJImage caption, Alfozan was captured looking behind a television where a device had been insertedWho is Abdulrahman Alfozan?Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. The complaint said he was educated in the US and has been a legal permanent resident since 2020.He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI has been terminated.Alfozan's lawyer William Pernik told the BBC: "Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream."These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why."Pernik added: "In the meantime, we respectfully ask everyone to withhold judgment until full facts become known. Like every one of us, Mr Alfozan is presumed innocent, and what has been made public is an accusation, not a finding of guilt." On Tuesday, Alfozan made his initial appearance in a federal court in California. A detention hearing is scheduled on 19 October to determine whether he should remain in custody while proceedings continue.The FBI investigation is ongoing.If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£190,000) fine.

schema.headline: Toilet paper and secret recorders: What we know about the arrest of the Saudi OpenAI engineer

title: Are the European 2027 Women's World Cup play-offs working?
description: One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.The Netherlan
body: One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate.Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0.Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively. So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off."Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday."For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on."Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that."The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December.Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1.It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process.England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain.They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley.England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary. Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations.In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group.When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 .That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story.England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament.The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group.A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025.There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign.Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high."What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify."I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is."What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams.Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting.Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision.But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority.

schema.headline: Are the European 2027 Women's World Cup play-offs working?

title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says
description: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporea
body: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities.All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said.Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added.Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz.The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water.The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula.Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday.Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added.Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February.At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization.The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time.However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency.One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September.The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping.

schema.headline: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz after being hit by projectile, Singapore says

title: Paid companionship grows as loneliness rises in China
description: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonelyFigure caption, Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary childr
body: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonelyFigure caption, Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'ByChina correspondent"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia."I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.Image caption, Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own.But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that."We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs."For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine.""The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.Image caption, Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents.The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile."After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.Image caption, Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit.But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood."I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as  a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic."Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves."So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."Image caption, Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals.At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee."If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province."We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.Image caption, Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan.He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said."We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude."The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback."Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity.Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly."It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said."I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy."I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

schema.headline: Paid companionship grows as loneliness rises in China
